paper.journal: The European Journal of Health Economics
paper.code_data_availability: No data- or code-availability statement appears in the article. …

registers.name_in_paper: The Danish Mental Health and Well-Being Survey 2016 (DMHWBS2016)
registers.role: treatment (WEMWBS score), one covariate (physical activity) and the sample frame
variables_mentioned: WEMWBS (14-item Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale, range 14–70)
level of physical activity (weekly or more; less than weekly)

registers.role: linkage (personal registration number) and sample linkage to registers
outcomes (hospitalization and outpatient costs; and, as stated in Appendix 1, sickness benefit transfers) and the Charlson Comorbidity Index / psychiatric diagnoses
variables_mentioned: ICD-10 diagnoses (F00-F99, X60–X84 for psychiatric conditions and self-injury; Z30 and Z76 excluded from costs)

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish National Health Service Register (NHSR)
registers.role: outcomes (general practitioner and specialist contact costs)
variables_mentioned: contacts with the primary care sector
national health insurance rates / fees for more than 200 individually priced services
prescription drugs acquired at Danish pharmacies

linkages: Survey respondents linked to Danish national registers via each respondent's anonymized civil registration number (CPR number), through Statistics Denmark
Statistics Denmark encrypts the CPR number before releasing data for research; all data are pseudonymized

sample.universe: A random population-based sample of Danish men and women aged 16 years and above, contacted by Statistics Denmark in October 2016
sample.unit_of_observation: individual survey respondent linked to registers (one observation per person, with costs aggregated over calendar years 2016 and 2017)
selection_rules: Statistics Denmark sent an electronic invitation to the sampled individuals in October 2016
3,508 people responded to the web-based survey between October 18, 2016 and November 13, 2016 (34% response rate)

Both models were based on the sample with no missing data (complete cases); missing data were mental well-being 174 (5.0%), age 10 (0.3%), marital status 10 (0.3%), employment status 7 (0.2%), physical activity 5 (0.1%), income 6.8% (kept as a 'missing' category)
For sickness benefit transfer outcomes the sample was restricted to the working-age population, i.e. 16–64 years old (N = 1839)
sample.period: Survey October–November 2016; register costs for the full years 2016 and 2017
sample.n_observations: 3,508 respondents (1,839 in the working-age sample used for sickness benefit transfers); the complete-case estimation N is not printed

construction_notes: All costs are in 2016/2017 prices (DKK) and were converted to USD PPP with an online conversion tool (2017 rates, IMF PPP values, 1 DKK = USD$0.13 PPP); main tables report USD PPP and Appendix 2 the original DKK

Healthcare costs comprise GP/specialist contacts (national health insurance rates), hospitalizations and outpatient services (DRG and DAGS charges) and prescription medicines (retail price minus user payments); costs omitted for services not involving treatment for illness (ICD-10 Z30, Z76) and for normal births, sterilization and healthy companions
Sickness benefit transfers cover long-term absence (31 + days, including partial transfers), estimated from the weekly number of hours absent from work and respective salaries
All costs aggregated separately for the full year 2016 and the full year 2017
Chronic conditions measured by the Charlson Comorbidity Index over 19 conditions, categorized low (CCI = 0), medium (CCI = 1–2), high (CCI ≥ 3)
Number of psychiatric conditions = count of psychiatric and self-injury diagnoses, ICD-10 F00-F99 and X60–X84, entered as a continuous variable
Income entered as quartiles with a 'missing' category for the 6.8% with missing income
All variables entered as categorical except age and the number of psychiatric conditions
A survey non-response statistical weight based on age, education, region, marital status, employment status and migration background was applied in all analyses
Variance inflation factors were computed for each independent variable; all VIFs were < 5

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: this is a prospective observational cohort in which variation in the 2016 WEMWBS score across survey respondents is related to register-measured costs in 2017, adjusting for observed covariates including costs in the previous year.

key_assumptions.assumption: No unmeasured confounding: mental well-being in 2016 is independent of the 2017 cost outcome's potential values once the measured covariates (including costs in the previous year) are conditioned on.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state the adjustment set was chosen to minimize confounding of health factors and note that the covariates are associated with both mental well-being and healthcare service utilization; no formal test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unmeasured health behaviours (alcohol consumption, smoking, nutrition) do not confound the mental well-being–cost association; the authors concede they could not adjust for them and that they may also be mediators.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No evidence offered; stated as a limitation.

key_assumptions.assumption: Temporal ordering: mental well-being is measured in 2016 and the cost outcome in 2017, so the 2017 costs cannot have caused the 2016 well-being score (no reverse causation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The prospective design is named as a major strength; the authors note, however, that there was some overlap between the time of the survey (October 2016) and the cost data (2016 and 2017).

key_assumptions.assumption: No overadjustment: conditioning on costs in the previous year (and, in model 2, on health status and health behaviour) does not block part of the association of interest.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors raise this as a possibility and argue the design is therefore conservative; no test.

key_assumptions.assumption: Survey non-response and complete-case restriction do not bias the association once the survey non-response weights are applied (34% response rate; response rates were higher for women, older, more educated, married, employed, Danish-background and higher-income individuals).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Non-response weights based on age, education, region, marital status, employment status and migration background; the authors nonetheless state selection bias cannot be ruled out.
